newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London ended mostly firmer showing little response to the draw-down in US certified coffee stocks and strong Brazilian exports. Front month November was $14 down at $1,495, while January was $12 up at $1,401 a tonne. Traders expect the large November premium against January to narrow further as sellers put up their coffee for tender to take advantage of the premium.

In New York arabica futures ended mixed with nearby contracts advancing after a late- session bout of commission house buying. December added 1.10 cents/lb to close at 118.85 cents/lb, while March ended 85 points higher at 107.90 cents/lb. The weekly certified stock data, which showed a decline of 743 60-kg bags in the week ended November 1, to 804 bags had, as anticipated, little impact on prices, as stocks are near nil anyhow.

According to broker GNI the world coffee market could be faced with a substantial supply deficit in 1997/98 (October/September) if consumption growth remains strong and forecasts of a lower Brazilian crop proved correct. GNI said there was a growing consensus that Brazil's 1997/98 crop, now at the flowering stage, would be lower than 1996/97's harvest of around 25 to 26 million 60-kg bags.

It was added that if supply and demand are in balance in 1996/97 then a deficit in the order of 6 million bags can be expected for 1997/98, if the Brazilian forecast is proved correct. GNI said while the combined stocks of the Brazilian government and the Colombian Coffee Federation were ample to offset the projected imbalance, they were unlikely to release sufficient stock unless prices dictated such action. Talk of a small Brazilian crop in 1997/98 has been circulating for some time and hence, the forecast is nothing new.

BRAZIL - Brazilian coffee exports for the month of October already total 1.707 million 60-kg bags based on bills of lading which already represents the highest monthly figure since September 1993. Exporters can continue, however, to ship through to November 10, using certificates of origin issued for October so that the final October figure will certainly be higher than the 1.7 million bags. Should final shipments match certificates of origin, then October shipments would be the highest for five years, stretching back to the 2.181 million bags exported in November 1991, according to FEBEC statistics.

October shipments have benefitted from a delay in finalisation of a state export tax exemption which took place in the middle of September after a lull in export activity the first two weeks of the month. However, the pace of shipments in October is not expected to be repeated in November and December.

GERMANY - Germany imported 980,714 bags of coffee in June 1996, nearly 14 per cent less than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 6.403 million bags, 1.8 per cent less than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 5.7 per cent to 12.9 million bags.

Major suppliers of green coffee in January/June 1996 were Ethiopia (312,800 vs 321,100 bags), Kenya (332,500 vs 247,600 bags), El Salvador (577,500 vs 525,000 bags), Guatemala (326,700 vs 251,900 bags), Honduras (392,700 vs 318,300 bags) and Colombia (1.345 vs 1.778 million bags).

The country exported 1.689 million bags of coffee in January/June 1996, 18 per cent more than was exported the same period in 1995. Total exports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 7.9 per cent to 3.238 million bags.
